meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Being Irish, he had an abiding sense of tragedy which sustained him through temporary periods of joy'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Yeats. Researchers find no such line in his work. The earliest match is a 1991 variant Oliver Stone credited to him — 50+ years after Yeats died.

answer.label: Not W. B. Yeats — an anonymous modern saying
answer.sourceLine: There is no Yeats source. Several researchers have tried and failed to find this sentence anywhere in Yeats’s published work, and the earliest match Quote Investigator located ↗ is a variant that film director Oliver Stone credited to Yeats in the San Francisco Chronicle in 1991 — more than fifty years after Yeats died in 1939. The familiar wording is first documented in 1993, and the originator remains anonymous.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: No. Researchers, including Yeats specialists, have failed to locate it
San Francisco Chronicle, 3 March 1991 — a variant quoted by Oliver Stone

source.excerpt: The Townes bring to mind a description of a countryman by poet William Butler Yeats: “Being Irish, he had an abiding sense of tragedy which sustained him through temporary periods of joy.”
trail: 1911 — Yeats writes of J. M. Synge’s love of “all that stings into life the sense of tragedy.” Real Yeats, real subject — but, as Quote Investigator notes ↗, no temporary periods of joy anywhere in it.

1991 — the earliest located match: Oliver Stone, promoting his Jim Morrison film, tells the San Francisco Chronicle that Morrison reminds him of “something William Butler Yeats said about another Irishman,” then gives a variant with an “itinerant sense of joy” — per QI’s citation ↗.

1993–1996 — the wording settles and the credit hardens: a Chicago Sun-Times review (1993), a Notre Dame football history (1994), a New York Times profile of a novelist who kept it on his bulletin board (1995), and an epigraph to Martha Manning’s Chasing Grace (1996), all naming Yeats. Chronology ↗.

2009 onward — the searches come back empty. A columnist canvasses professors including a leading Yeats scholar and finds no original; Yeats scholar Neil Mann later files the line under misattributions ↗ as “source uncertain, but not Yeats.”
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest appearance of the familiar wording that Quote Investigator has located ↗, in a book review by Dolores and Roger Flaherty. The Yeats credit inside it is the unsupported part: the columnists are passing the line on, not sourcing it.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted, because no origin is known. The line cannot be tied to any work by Yeats, so it is not covered by the public-domain status of his pre-1931 writing; and the earliest documented appearances are 1990s newspaper and book texts by identifiable living authors, which are themselves in copyright. Treat the sentence as an unsourced modern saying of unknown authorship.

author.name: W. B. Yeats
author.heading: About the name it gets pinned on
author.metaLine: 1865–1939 · Irish poet & dramatist · Nobel Prize in Literature, 1923
author.bio: William Butler Yeats was born in Sandymount, County Dublin on 13 June 1865 and died at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin in France on 28 January 1939. He co-founded the Abbey Theatre in 1904 with Lady Gregory and J. M. Synge, sat in the Irish Senate from 1922, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923. He is also one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for unsourced ‘Irish’ aphorisms — a Yeats scholar’s own list of misattributions includes this line alongside ‘Education is not the filling of a pail’ and several sayings that belong to other writers entirely.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source exists. See Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: Being Irish, He Had an Abiding Sense of Tragedy Which Sustained Him Through Temporary Periods of Joy,” 21 March 2023.

misattribution.heading: The fact-check
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared ‘Yeats’ lines on the internet, and there is no evidence he wrote a word of it. Here is what the record actually shows.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ reports that several researchers have unsuccessfully attempted to locate the statement in Yeats’s works and calls the ascription currently unsupported. Its earliest located match is from 1991, more than fifty years after Yeats died in 1939. The line also does not appear among Wikiquote’s sourced Yeats quotations ↗.
Yeats scholar Neil Mann includes it in his own list of Yeats misattributions ↗ with the note “source uncertain, but not Yeats” — and offers no alternative author.

Quote Investigator records “itinerant sense of joy” (1991), “Being depressed…” billed as an old Irish adage (1994), “transient periods of joy” (1995 and 1996), and even “A Norwegian has an abiding sense of TRAGEDY” on a piece of gift-shop calligraphy (2001). See the chronology ↗. Sayings with a real text do not wander like this.

In a Providence College commencement speech the novelist applied the description to Yeats rather than crediting it to him. Quote Investigator observes that a passage like that would have facilitated a misattribution through inattentiveness — while noting it has not yet found such a passage before 1991 ↗, so this is a mechanism, not a proven origin.
Goodreads ↗ carries it under Yeats with 573 likes and no source at all, beneath its own notice that quotes are added by the community and not verified.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who wrote it. Quote Investigator ↗ believes the ascription to Yeats is incorrect, suspects a citation earlier than 1991 will eventually surface, and concludes that for now the originator remains anonymous.

context.heading: Why this one sticks
lead: The joke is built backwards, and that is why it travels. Tragedy is supposed to interrupt joy; here joy is the interruption, and tragedy is the load-bearing wall. It reads exactly like the kind of rueful Irish epigram Yeats could have written, which is most of what a misattribution needs.

Yeats did write about Irishness and tragedy — his 1911 essay on J. M. Synge praises Synge’s love of “all that stings into life the sense of tragedy” — but, as Quote Investigator notes ↗, he says nothing there about temporary periods of joy. The nearest real Yeats sentence is a genuine sentiment that the fake sharpens into a punchline.
context.detailsSummary: The 2009 search that came up empty — and the ‘Norwegian’ variant
detailsBody: In 2009 the Cleveland columnist Ted Diadiun went looking for the original. As Quote Investigator quotes him ↗, he searched books and the web, asked several university professors including a leading Yeats scholar, and found that some had heard of the line but none had ever seen it in an original work. His conclusion is the best short description of how quotation myths harden: thousands of people online “know” Yeats wrote it, and what they actually know is that thousands of others “know” the same thing.

The saying is also detachable from Ireland altogether. Quote Investigator records a 2001 memoir describing a framed piece of calligraphy in a Wisconsin gift shop that read “A Norwegian has an abiding sense of TRAGEDY which sustains him through temporary periods of JOY.” A line that swaps nationalities that easily was never anchored to a text.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the ascription to W. B. Yeats is unsupported and incorrect, that the originator remains anonymous, that its earliest located match is Oliver Stone in the San Francisco Chronicle of 3 March 1991 using an 'itinerant sense of joy' variant more than fifty years after Yeats's death, that the familiar wording first appears in the Chicago Sun-Times of 7 March 1993 (Dolores and Roger Flaherty), and it records the 1911 Synge essay, the 1994 'Being depressed' variant, the 1995 'transient' and New York Times citations, the 1996 Manning epigraph and Mary Higgins Clark speech, the 2001 'A Norwegian' calligraphy, and Ted Diadiun's 2009 failed search.
Yeats scholar Neil Mann's blog The Widening Gyre lists the line among Yeats misattributions with the note 'source uncertain, but not Yeats' and offers no alternative attribution.
Wikiquote's William Butler Yeats page does not contain 'abiding sense of tragedy' or 'temporary periods of joy' anywhere among its sourced quotations.
Goodreads lists the quote as by William Butler Yeats with no book or source cited, with 573 likes, under a notice that quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.

W. B. Yeats was born 13 June 1865 in Sandymount, County Dublin and died 28 January 1939 at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, France; he won the 1923 Nobel Prize in Literature, co-founded the Abbey Theatre in 1904 with Lady Gregory and J. M. Synge, and served in the Irish Senate from December 1922.
Project Gutenberg hosts free full texts under the author entry 'Yeats, W. B. (William Butler) 1865-1939'.
